entries.term: with + object + -ing: With prices rising, …
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *With* + noun + *-ing* sets the background situation for the main clause, often as a reason: *With prices rising, people are spending less.*
entries.usage: Common in news, business writing and conversation; it is lighter than a full *because* or *since* clause and usually describes an ongoing situation. The noun after *with* is the subject of the *-ing* verb, so it can be different from the main subject. For a negative, use *with no one* + *-ing* or *with* + noun + *not* + *-ing*.
entries.pattern: With + noun / pronoun + -ing …, main clause
examples: **With prices rising** every month, a lot of families are cutting back on eating out.
**With my in-laws visiting** for the week, our little apartment feels pretty crowded.
**With the deadline approaching**, the whole team worked through the weekend.

drill.sentence: {{With the rain getting heavier}}, we decided to turn back and try the trail another day.
drill.hint: Rewrite with with + noun + -ing: Because the rain was getting heavier, we decided to turn back and try the trail another day.

mistake.wrong: With the economy is slowing down, companies are hiring less.
mistake.right: With the economy slowing down, companies are hiring less.
mistake.why: *With* takes a noun + *-ing* form, not a full clause; drop *is*, or use *because* + a full clause.

entries.term: reduced adverbial clause: if needed, once finished, when in doubt
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: After *if, when, once, unless* and *while*, the subject and a form of *be* can be left out when they are clear from context: *if (it is) needed*, *once (it is) finished*.
entries.usage: Very common in instructions, emails and labels, where it sounds compact and practical (*Call me if needed*). Many are fixed phrases: *if necessary, if possible, when in doubt, unless otherwise noted*. Only the subject and *be* disappear, so other verbs must stay (*if you have questions*, not *if questions*).
entries.pattern: if / when / once / unless / while + past participle / adjective / prepositional phrase
examples: Feel free to call me over the weekend **if needed**.
**Once finished**, the new bridge will cut twenty minutes off the commute.
**When in doubt**, ask the pharmacist before mixing two medications.

drill.sentence: Keep the jar in the fridge {{once opened}} and use it within two weeks.
drill.hint: Shorten the time clause: Keep the jar in the fridge once it is opened and use it within two weeks.

mistake.wrong: If any questions, please let me know.
mistake.right: If you have any questions, please let me know.
mistake.why: Only a subject and *be* can be dropped (*if needed* = if it is needed); a clause with *have* must stay complete.

entries.term: not as a clause substitute: I hope not / I guess not
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: After *hope, guess, suppose* and *be afraid*, *not* replaces a whole negative clause: *Will it rain? – I hope not* means *I hope it won't rain*.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation and casual emails. With *hope* and *be afraid*, only *not* works (*I hope not*, never *I don't hope so*); with *think*, the normal form is *I don't think so*, and *I think not* sounds formal or dramatic. *I'm afraid not* is the polite way to give bad news or say no.
entries.pattern: I hope / guess / suppose / 'm afraid + not
examples: "Are we going to miss our flight?" "**I hope not**, but this traffic is terrible."
"So you won't make it to dinner?" "**I guess not**. This meeting is running really late."
"Is the water damage covered by our insurance?" "**I'm afraid not**."

drill.sentence: "Do you think it'll snow tomorrow?" "{{I hope not}}. I have to drive to Denver."
drill.hint: Answer briefly, replacing the negative clause: I hope it won't snow.

mistake.wrong: "Is it going to rain?" "I don't hope so."
mistake.right: "Is it going to rain?" "I hope not."
mistake.why: With *hope*, the negative goes into *not*: *I hope not*; *I don't hope so* is not used.

entries.term: ellipsis after auxiliaries: I could have, but I didn't
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: After an auxiliary or a modal, the rest of the verb phrase is left out when it repeats something just said: *I could have called, but I didn't.*
entries.usage: Natural in all registers; repeating the verb usually sounds clumsy. Use *do / does / did* when the first verb has no auxiliary (*She likes jazz, and I do too*), and after a modal keep *be* and perfect *have* (*He should be*, *I could have*). The final auxiliary is stressed and cannot be contracted (*Yes, I have*, not *Yes, I've*).
entries.pattern: subject + auxiliary / modal (+ have / be), rest of the verb phrase left out
examples: I **could have** taken the job in Seattle, but I **didn't**.
"Have you ever been to Alaska?" "No, but my parents **have**."
He isn't nearly as worried about the surgery as he **should be**.

drill.sentence: They didn't invite us to the wedding, but they really {{should have}}.
drill.hint: Avoid repeating the verb: They didn't invite us to the wedding, but they really should have invited us.

mistake.wrong: "Have you finished?" "Yes, I've."
mistake.right: "Have you finished?" "Yes, I have."
mistake.why: An auxiliary at the end of a clause carries the stress, so it cannot be contracted.

entries.term: to-infinitive ellipsis: I'd love to
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *To* stays but the verb after it is left out when that verb was just mentioned: *Do you want to come? – I'd love to.*
entries.usage: Natural in all registers after *want, would like, would love, need, have, used, be going* and *ought*: *to* stays and the verb goes (*I don't want to*, *We were going to*). *To* can be dropped after *try* (*I'll try*) and in set phrases like *if you want* and *whenever you like*.
entries.pattern: want / love / need / try / used / be going + to (the verb after to is left out)
examples: "Want to grab dinner after work?" "**I'd love to**, but I promised to call my mom tonight."
You don't have to come to the reunion if you don't **want to**.
We're not moving to Chicago after all. We **were going to**, but then my wife got a great offer here.

drill.sentence: I don't eat much meat these days, but I {{used to}}.
drill.hint: Avoid repeating the verb: I don't eat much meat these days, but I used to eat a lot of it.

mistake.wrong: "Would you like to join us?" "Yes, I'd like."
mistake.right: "Would you like to join us?" "Yes, I'd like to."
mistake.why: *Would like* and *would love* need *to* when the verb after them is left out: *I'd like to*, *I'd love to*.

entries.term: situational ellipsis in speech: Sounds good. / Want some?
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: In casual speech, words that are clear from the situation, usually the subject and auxiliary, are dropped at the start of a sentence: *(That) sounds good*, *(Do you) want some?*
entries.usage: Very common in conversation, texts and chat messages, where it sounds friendly and relaxed: *Got it*, *Want some?*, *Seen my keys?*, *Hope you're well*. Only the beginning of the sentence is dropped, never words in the middle. Avoid it in formal emails and documents.
entries.pattern: (subject + auxiliary) left out: Sounds good / Want some? / Got a minute?
examples: "I'll pick up the pizza on my way home." "**Sounds good**. I'll set the table."
I just made a fresh pot of coffee. **Want some**?
**Got a minute**? I need your opinion on something before I hit send.

drill.sentence: "I'll bring the drinks, and you bring dessert." "{{Sounds like a plan}}."
drill.hint: Reply casually, dropping the subject: That sounds like a plan.

mistake.wrong: Sound good, see you at seven.
mistake.right: Sounds good, see you at seven.
mistake.why: The dropped subject is *that*, so the statement keeps the *-s*; *Sound good?* without *-s* works only as a question (*Does that sound good?*).

entries.term: no matter how / what / who
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: Says that the main statement stays true in every case, whatever the degree, thing or person: *No matter how hard I try, I can't …*
entries.usage: Very common in speech and writing; *however* + adjective (*however late*) means the same but sounds more formal. An adjective or adverb stays right after *how* (*no matter how late it is*), and the clause uses the present tense for future meaning. *No matter what* can also stand alone at the end (*I'll be there, no matter what*).
entries.pattern: No matter + how + adjective / adverb, what, who, where + clause, main clause
examples: **No matter how early** I leave, I always hit traffic on the bridge.
**No matter what** the critics say, I loved that movie.
**No matter who** wins tonight, the city is going to party until morning.

drill.sentence: {{No matter how much}} I sleep, I'm always exhausted on Monday mornings.
drill.hint: Rewrite with no matter: It doesn't matter how much I sleep; I'm always exhausted on Monday mornings.

mistake.wrong: No matter what will happen, I'll support you.
mistake.right: No matter what happens, I'll support you.
mistake.why: Like other condition clauses, a *no matter* clause uses the present tense for the future, not *will*.

entries.term: sentence relative which: …, which surprised me
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: A *which*-clause after a comma can refer to the whole previous clause, not just the last noun: *He apologized, which surprised me* means that his apology surprised me.
entries.usage: Very common in speech and writing for adding a comment, a reaction or a result. It always follows a comma, and *that* or *what* cannot replace *which* here. In casual speech, *which* sometimes starts a new sentence (*Which is fine*), but avoid this in formal writing.
entries.pattern: clause, which + verb (a comment on the whole clause)
examples: My flight was canceled, **which meant** I had to spend the night at the airport.
She paid for everyone's dinner, **which was** really generous of her.
The city lowered the speed limit to 25, **which has made** our street a lot safer.

drill.sentence: He forgot my birthday again, {{which}} really hurt.
drill.hint: Join into one sentence with a comment clause: He forgot my birthday again. That really hurt.

mistake.wrong: He didn't call back, what made me nervous.
mistake.right: He didn't call back, which made me nervous.
mistake.why: To comment on a whole clause, use *which*; *what* cannot point back to something already said.

entries.term: which is why …
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: Gives a result of the whole previous statement: *X, which is why Y* means *X, and that is the reason for Y*.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation, emails and explanations, because it keeps cause and result in one smooth sentence. It is close to *so*, but it puts more weight on the reason. Starting a new sentence with *Which is why* is fine in speech, but in formal writing *That is why* is safer.
entries.pattern: clause, which is why + clause
examples: Our kitchen is tiny, **which is why** we eat out so often.
My manager hates long emails, **which is why** I always put the main point first.
The bridge was closed for repairs, **which is why** traffic was so bad downtown.

drill.sentence: The tickets sold out in minutes, {{which is why}} we're watching the game at home.
drill.hint: Join with a relative clause: The tickets sold out in minutes. That's why we're watching the game at home.

mistake.wrong: It was raining, that's why we stayed in.
mistake.right: It was raining, which is why we stayed in.
mistake.why: In writing, *that's why* cannot join two clauses with only a comma; use *which is why* or start a new sentence.

entries.term: that vs. which in restrictive clauses (US)
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: In edited American English, *that* introduces defining clauses, with no commas, and *which* introduces extra information, after a comma.
entries.usage: Most American editors and style guides (AP, Chicago) follow this rule, but *which* in defining clauses is normal in British English, appears in much published American writing, and is not a grammar error. Commas change the meaning: *the cars that were damaged* (only some) vs. *the cars, which were damaged* (all of them). In clauses between commas, *that* is never possible.
entries.pattern: noun + that … (defining, no commas) / noun, which … (extra information, commas)
examples: The apartment **that** we liked best was already taken.
My grandmother's recipe book, **which** she wrote entirely by hand, is now falling apart.
Please send me the version **that** includes the final budget numbers.

drill.sentence: The shoes {{that}} I ordered online don't fit, so I'm sending them back.
drill.hint: Choose that or which (American style, no commas): The shoes ___ I ordered online don't fit, so I'm sending them back.

mistake.wrong: The report, that I sent yesterday, has a mistake in it.
mistake.right: The report, which I sent yesterday, has a mistake in it.
mistake.why: *That* cannot introduce a clause between commas; extra information needs *which* (or *who* for people).

entries.term: the fact that …
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: Turns a whole clause into a noun phrase, so it can follow a preposition or act as the subject: *despite the fact that …*, *The fact that he lied …*
entries.usage: Needed after most prepositions, because a *that*-clause cannot follow them directly (*despite the fact that he …*, not *despite that he …*). It is also common as a subject (*The fact that nobody noticed is worrying*). Editors often cut it when a shorter form works: *although* for *despite the fact that*, *because* for *due to the fact that*.
entries.pattern: preposition + the fact that + clause / The fact that + clause + verb
examples: **The fact that** she remembered my name after ten years really touched me.
I'm still getting used to **the fact that** my son is old enough to drive.
Many neighbors are upset about **the fact that** the new park still has no restrooms.

drill.sentence: The trip was a lot of fun {{in spite of the fact that}} it rained every day.
drill.hint: Rewrite with in spite of: The trip was a lot of fun, although it rained every day.

mistake.wrong: We talked about that the rent is going up.
mistake.right: We talked about the fact that the rent is going up.
mistake.why: A preposition cannot be followed directly by a *that*-clause; add *the fact*, or rephrase (*We talked about the rent going up*).

entries.term: comparative correlative: The more …, the more …
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: Two linked comparatives show that two things change together: *The more you practice, the easier it gets.*
entries.usage: Common in speech and writing, and in short fixed forms like *The more, the merrier* and *The sooner, the better*. Each half starts with *the* + comparative, and the comparative takes its noun or adjective with it to the front (*the more money …*, *the more careful …*). The first half works like an *if*-clause, so it uses the present for the future.
entries.pattern: The + comparative (+ subject + verb), the + comparative (+ subject + verb)
examples: **The more** I learn about wine, **the less** I feel I know.
**The longer** you wait to fix a leak, **the more expensive** it gets.
"Can I bring a couple of friends?" "Sure, **the more, the merrier**."

drill.sentence: {{The more you exercise, the better}} you sleep.
drill.hint: Rewrite with the …, the …: If you exercise more, you sleep better.

mistake.wrong: The more you earn money, the more you spend.
mistake.right: The more money you earn, the more you spend.
mistake.why: *More* takes its noun with it to the front of the clause: *the more money you earn*.

entries.term: as + past participle: as mentioned, as discussed
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: A short *as*-clause that points back to something said, written or agreed earlier: *As mentioned* means *as I mentioned* or *as was mentioned*.
entries.usage: Very common in emails, reports and presentations (*As discussed on Friday, …*; *as shown in Table 2*). It sounds efficient and professional; *as previously mentioned* is more formal, and *like I said* is the casual spoken version. *As expected* and *as planned* work the same way.
entries.pattern: As + past participle (+ earlier / above / on Monday), main clause
examples: **As discussed** on Monday, the office will be closed the Friday after Thanksgiving.
**As shown** in Figure 3, the error rate drops sharply after the first few training epochs.
**As expected**, the storm knocked out power across most of the county.

drill.sentence: {{As agreed}}, I'll pick up the kids on Wednesdays and you'll take Fridays.
drill.hint: Shorten the as-clause: As we agreed, I'll pick up the kids on Wednesdays and you'll take Fridays.

mistake.wrong: As it was mentioned above, the deadline is Friday.
mistake.right: As mentioned above, the deadline is Friday.
mistake.why: In the short form, the participle follows *as* directly; *as it was mentioned* mixes it with the full form *as I mentioned*.

entries.term: reduced comparative: than expected, than usual
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: After *than* (and *as*), the subject and verb are often left out when they are obvious: *longer than expected* means *longer than we expected*.
entries.usage: Very common in news, reports and everyday speech (*It took longer than expected*). The usual fixed forms are *than expected, than usual, than necessary, than planned* and *than ever*. The full form (*than we had expected*) is also correct, just longer.
entries.pattern: comparative + than + expected / usual / necessary / planned / ever
examples: The kitchen remodel took twice as long and cost much more **than expected**.
Traffic was lighter **than usual**, so I got to the office twenty minutes early.
Don't use more salt **than necessary**; people can always add it at the table.

drill.sentence: The concert ended much later {{than planned}}, so we missed the last train home.
drill.hint: Shorten the comparison: The concert ended much later than the organizers had planned, so we missed the last train home.

mistake.wrong: Traffic is heavier than usually this morning.
mistake.right: Traffic is heavier than usual this morning.
mistake.why: The fixed phrase is *than usual*, with the adjective, just like *as usual*.

entries.term: let alone: I can't boil an egg, let alone cook dinner
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: Means *and certainly not*: after a negative statement, it adds a bigger or less likely case: *I can't afford a car, let alone a house.*
entries.usage: Common in speech and writing. The first part is negative or nearly negative (*hardly, barely, never, too tired to*), and the item after *let alone* matches the grammar of the part it is compared with (*can't walk, let alone run*). *Much less* means the same and sounds a little more formal.
entries.pattern: negative clause, let alone + matching word or phrase
examples: I can barely afford rent, **let alone** a vacation in Hawaii.
He's never cooked a real meal, **let alone** Thanksgiving dinner for twelve.
Most Americans have never heard of the town, **let alone** visited it.

drill.sentence: My grandfather doesn't use email, {{let alone}} social media.
drill.hint: Add a stronger case (not *much less* or *never mind*): My grandfather doesn't use email. He certainly doesn't use social media.

mistake.wrong: I can run five miles, let alone a marathon.
mistake.right: I can't run five miles, let alone a marathon.
mistake.why: *Let alone* follows a negative statement; after a positive one it makes no sense.

entries.term: only to + verb (unexpected result): …, only to find …
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: Introduces a disappointing or surprising result that followed an action: *We drove two hours, only to find the museum closed.*
entries.usage: Typical of storytelling and news writing; it usually follows a comma. The verb is often *find, discover, learn, realize* or *be told*. Unlike a normal *to*-infinitive, it does not express purpose: nobody drove two hours in order to find the museum closed.
entries.pattern: clause, only to + find / discover / learn / be told …
examples: She studied for weeks, **only to discover** the exam had been moved to the spring.
The startup raised millions of dollars, **only to collapse** two years later.
We hiked all the way to the top, **only to find** the view completely hidden by clouds.

drill.sentence: I finally got to the front of the line, {{only to be told}} that tickets were sold out.
drill.hint: Rewrite with only to: I finally got to the front of the line, and then I was told that tickets were sold out.

mistake.wrong: We hurried to the station, only to found that the train had left.
mistake.right: We hurried to the station, only to find that the train had left.
mistake.why: After *to*, always use the base form, even when the story is in the past.

entries.term: object it before if: I'd appreciate it if …
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: Verbs like *appreciate, like, love* and *hate* need the object *it* before an *if*- or *when*-clause: *I'd appreciate it if you could reply by Friday.*
entries.usage: Very common in polite requests in emails and speech. *It* stands for the situation in the clause, which usually has *could*, *would* or a past form (*I'd appreciate it if you didn't tell anyone*). The same pattern gives *I hate it when* and *I love it when*.
entries.pattern: appreciate / like / love / hate + it + if / when + clause
examples: **I'd appreciate it if** you could send me the invoice by Friday.
**I hate it when** people talk on their phones during a movie.
My mom would **love it if** we came home for Thanksgiving this year.

drill.sentence: {{I'd appreciate it if you didn't}} mention this to anyone yet.
drill.hint: Make it a polite request with appreciate and a past verb: Please don't mention this to anyone yet.

mistake.wrong: I would appreciate if you could help me.
mistake.right: I would appreciate it if you could help me.
mistake.why: *Appreciate* needs an object, so *it* must come before the *if*-clause.

entries.term: present participle clause: Walking home, I …
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: An *-ing* clause without a conjunction can replace a time or reason clause when its subject is the same as the main subject: *Walking home, I saw …* means *While I was walking home, I saw …*
entries.usage: Common in written stories, journalism and careful speech; in conversation people usually prefer a full clause with *when*, *while* or *because*. The clause can also follow the main clause (*She left, slamming the door*). It suggests that the two actions happen at the same time or one right after the other.
entries.pattern: -ing clause, subject + verb / subject + verb, -ing clause
examples: **Walking home** from the station, I ran into my old high school teacher.
**Feeling** a little sick, she decided to skip the party and go to bed early.
He sat by the window for hours, **watching** the snow pile up on the street.

drill.sentence: {{Wanting}} to save money, I took the bus instead of a cab.
drill.hint: Shorten with a participle clause: Because I wanted to save money, I took the bus instead of a cab.

mistake.wrong: Because being new in town, he didn't know anyone at the party.
mistake.right: Being new in town, he didn't know anyone at the party.
mistake.why: *Because* needs a full clause (*because he was new in town*); the *-ing* clause gives the reason on its own.

entries.term: negative participle clause: Not knowing what to say, …
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *Not* + *-ing* gives a reason or a background situation in the negative: *Not knowing what to say, I stayed quiet* means *Because I didn't know what to say, I stayed quiet*.
entries.usage: Typical of written narrative and careful speech; in conversation people more often say *Since I didn't know …*. *Not* normally comes before the participle, including *being* and *having* (*Not being sure …*, *Not having heard back …*). Common verbs are *know, want, have, be sure* and *realize*.
entries.pattern: Not + -ing (or Not having + past participle) …, subject + verb
examples: **Not knowing** anyone at the party, I spent most of the night talking to the dog.
**Not wanting** to wake the baby, we whispered all through dinner.
**Not having heard** back from the landlord, she called him again on Monday morning.

drill.sentence: {{Not having}} a car, he biked to work every day, even in winter.
drill.hint: Shorten with a participle clause: Since he didn't have a car, he biked to work every day, even in winter.

mistake.wrong: Being not sure what to do, I called my brother.
mistake.right: Not being sure what to do, I called my brother.
mistake.why: In a participle clause, *not* goes before the *-ing* form, even before *being*.

entries.term: past participle clause: Built in 1890, the house …
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: A clause that starts with a past participle has a passive meaning and describes the subject of the main clause: *Built in 1890, the house …* means *The house, which was built in 1890, …*
entries.usage: Common in writing: news, guidebooks, real estate listings and biographies; it is rare in casual speech. The main subject must be the thing that receives the action (the house was built), or the sentence dangles. It can also give a reason or a condition (*Used carefully, this knife will last for years*).
entries.pattern: past participle (+ by / in / for …), subject (the receiver of the action) + verb
examples: **Built in 1890**, the house still has its original wood floors.
**Written** in just six weeks, her first novel became a surprise bestseller.
**Asked** about his future, the coach said only that he needed a long rest.

drill.sentence: {{Served}} with fresh bread, the soup makes a perfect winter lunch.
drill.hint: Shorten with a participle clause: When it is served with fresh bread, the soup makes a perfect winter lunch.

mistake.wrong: Building in 1890, the house has a long history.
mistake.right: Built in 1890, the house has a long history.
mistake.why: The house did not build anything; for a passive meaning, use the past participle.

entries.term: perfect participle clause: Having finished …, she …
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *Having* + past participle shows that the first action was complete before the main action, and often that it explains it: *Having finished the report, she went home.*
entries.usage: Formal or written style; in speech people say *After she finished …* or *Once she'd finished …*. Use it mainly when the order matters or when the first action is the reason for the second (*Having lost his keys twice, he now keeps a spare*). The passive form is *having been* + past participle.
entries.pattern: Having (+ been) + past participle …, subject + verb
examples: **Having lived** in Tokyo for ten years, she speaks fluent Japanese.
**Having missed** the last bus, we had to walk home in the rain.
**Having been** injured twice last season, the quarterback isn't taking any risks.

drill.sentence: {{Having paid}} the bill, she grabbed her coat and left the restaurant.
drill.hint: Shorten with a perfect participle: After she had paid the bill, she grabbed her coat and left the restaurant.

mistake.wrong: Finished the report, she went home.
mistake.right: Having finished the report, she went home.
mistake.why: A completed action done by the subject needs *having*; a bare past participle at the start reads as passive.

entries.term: while / when + -ing: While living in Berlin, …
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: Keeping *while*, *when*, *after*, *before* or *since* before an *-ing* form makes the time relation clear: *While living in Berlin, I learned German.*
entries.usage: Common in writing and careful speech, and clearer than a bare *-ing* clause. *After* and *before* + *-ing* are normal even in casual speech; *while* and *when* + *-ing* are common in instructions and warnings (*Don't text while driving*) but otherwise sound a little written. The implied subject of the *-ing* form must be the main subject.
entries.pattern: while / when / after / before / since + -ing …, subject + verb
examples: **While living** in Berlin, I picked up enough German to get by.
Be careful **when using** a ladder on wet ground.
**After moving** to Denver, they both took up skiing.

drill.sentence: {{While jogging}} in the park this morning, I lost my phone.
drill.hint: Shorten the time clause: While I was jogging in the park this morning, I lost my phone.

mistake.wrong: When arrived at the airport, we couldn't find our driver.
mistake.right: When we arrived at the airport, we couldn't find our driver.
mistake.why: After *when*, use a full clause (*when we arrived*) or an *-ing* form (*when arriving*); a past-tense verb cannot follow without its subject.

entries.term: reduced concessive: Although exhausted, she …
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *Although* or *though* + an adjective or participle, without subject and *be*, concedes a point: *Although exhausted, she finished the race* means *although she was exhausted*.
entries.usage: Typical of writing, news and reviews; it sounds compact and slightly formal. *Though* works the same way (*Though rare, side effects can be serious*), and so does *if* inside a noun phrase (*a bold, if risky, plan*). The implied subject must be the main subject.
entries.pattern: Although / Though + adjective / past participle, subject + verb
examples: **Although exhausted** after her night shift, the nurse stayed to help with a new patient.
**Though small**, the apartment gets great light all day.
**Although** clearly **nervous**, he gave a great toast at his brother's wedding.

drill.sentence: {{Although expensive}}, the dinner was worth every penny.
drill.hint: Shorten the concession: Although it was expensive, the dinner was worth every penny.

mistake.wrong: Despite tired, she kept running.
mistake.right: Although tired, she kept running.
mistake.why: *Despite* is a preposition and needs a noun or *-ing* form (*despite being tired*); only *although* and *though* take a bare adjective.

entries.term: reduced relative with -ing: people living nearby
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: An active relative clause is shortened to an *-ing* participle after the noun: *people living nearby* means *people who live nearby*.
entries.usage: Very common in news and reports, and natural in speech too (*the guy sitting next to you*). It works for ongoing actions and for states, even with verbs not normally used in the progressive (*a bag containing cash*). It cannot replace a clause about one finished action in the past: *the man who called yesterday*, not *the man calling yesterday*.
entries.pattern: noun + -ing … (= noun + who / that + active verb)
examples: Residents **living** near the airport have complained about night flights for years.
Who's the guy **sitting** next to your sister?
I found a shoebox **containing** all of my grandfather's old letters.

drill.sentence: Anyone {{wanting}} a refund should keep the original receipt.
drill.hint: Shorten the relative clause: Anyone who wants a refund should keep the original receipt.

mistake.wrong: The woman calling yesterday didn't leave a number.
mistake.right: The woman who called yesterday didn't leave a number.
mistake.why: An *-ing* participle cannot replace a relative clause about one finished action in the past; use a full clause.

entries.term: reduced relative with -ed: the data collected in 2020
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: A passive relative clause is shortened to a past participle after the noun: *the data collected in 2020* means *the data that was collected in 2020*.
entries.usage: Very common in academic writing, news and reports, and natural in speech (*the car parked outside*). A participle with extra words follows the noun (*the photos taken in Rome*); a single participle usually comes before it (*a broken window*), except in set uses like *the people involved*.
entries.pattern: noun + past participle (+ by / in / at …)
examples: All the **data collected** in 2020 had to be cleaned again after we found the sensor bug.
Most of the photos **taken** on our honeymoon are still on my old phone.
The car **parked** in front of our driveway has been there since Friday.

drill.sentence: The food {{left over from the party}} went to a local shelter.
drill.hint: Shorten the relative clause: The food that was left over from the party went to a local shelter.

mistake.wrong: The photos were taken in Rome are beautiful.
mistake.right: The photos taken in Rome are beautiful.
mistake.why: Drop both *that* and *were*; keeping *were* alone gives the sentence two main verbs.

entries.term: the first / last / only … to + verb
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: After *the first, the last, the only, the next* and superlatives, a *to*-infinitive can replace a relative clause: *She was the first to arrive* means *She was the first person who arrived*.
entries.usage: Common in all registers and usually more natural than the relative clause. The time comes from the main verb, so the same form works for past, present and future. The passive is *to be* + past participle (*the last to be told*).
entries.pattern: the first / last / only / next / superlative (+ noun) + to + verb
examples: My dad is always **the first to arrive** at family parties.
Why am I always **the last to know** about these things?
She was **the youngest player** ever **to win** the tournament.

drill.sentence: My grandmother was the first woman in her town {{to get}} a driver's license.
drill.hint: Shorten the relative clause: My grandmother was the first woman in her town who got a driver's license.

mistake.wrong: She was the first in her family going to college.
mistake.right: She was the first in her family to go to college.
mistake.why: After *the first*, *the last* and *the only*, use a *to*-infinitive, not an *-ing* form.

entries.term: dangling participle (error): Walking home, the rain started
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: A participle clause dangles when its implied subject is not the subject of the main clause: *Walking home, the rain started* says that the rain was walking home.
entries.usage: Editors and teachers treat it as an error in writing, because it can be unclear or unintentionally funny; in speech, listeners often don't notice. Fix it by making the doer the main subject (*Walking home, I got caught in the rain*) or by using a full clause (*As I was walking home, …*). Fixed openers like *judging by* and *considering* are accepted exceptions.
entries.pattern: -ing / -ed clause, + main subject = the doer of the participle
examples: **Running** for the bus, **I** slipped on the ice and broke my wrist.
**Looking** out the window, **we** could see the whole valley covered in snow.
**Born** in Ohio, **my father** moved to Texas as a teenager.

drill.sentence: {{When I opened the fridge}}, a terrible smell hit me.
drill.hint: Fix the dangling participle with a when-clause: Opening the fridge, a terrible smell hit me.

mistake.wrong: Driving through the park, the leaves looked beautiful.
mistake.right: Driving through the park, we admired the beautiful leaves.
mistake.why: The leaves were not driving; the main subject must be the person who does the action of the participle.

entries.term: accepted dangling participles: Judging by …, Considering …
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: Some participles work as fixed sentence openers and need no matching subject: *judging by, considering, given, assuming, generally speaking, speaking of*.
entries.usage: They act like prepositions or conjunctions, so editors accept them even when the main subject is different (*Judging by the sky, it's going to rain*). They are common in both speech and writing. *Based on* at the start of a sentence is very common too, but some editors still flag it.
entries.pattern: Judging by / Considering / Given / Assuming / Speaking of + noun or clause, main clause
examples: **Judging by** the line outside, this place must be really good.
**Considering** how little he trained, he ran a pretty good race.
**Speaking of** vacations, have you booked anything for the summer yet?

drill.sentence: {{Considering}} how old it is, the car still runs really well.
drill.hint: Start with a fixed -ing opener: When you think about how old it is, the car still runs really well.

mistake.wrong: Considering about the cost, we chose the cheaper hotel.
mistake.right: Considering the cost, we chose the cheaper hotel.
mistake.why: *Considering* takes its object directly, with no *about*.

entries.term: with + object + past participle: with his eyes closed
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *With* + noun + past participle describes the state of something during the main action, or a finished condition: *He listened with his eyes closed.*
entries.usage: Common in descriptions, stories and sports reporting (*with two players injured*). The participle has a passive meaning: the eyes are closed, the bills are paid. Compare *with* + noun + *-ing* for an ongoing action (*with prices rising*).
entries.pattern: with + noun + past participle
examples: He sat on the porch **with his arms folded**, waiting for an apology.
**With two starters injured**, the coach had to change the whole lineup.
**With the bills paid**, we finally had a little money left for a weekend trip.

drill.sentence: She drove all the way to the beach {{with the windows rolled down}}.
drill.hint: Rewrite with with: She drove all the way to the beach, and the windows were rolled down.

mistake.wrong: He listened with his eyes closing.
mistake.right: He listened with his eyes closed.
mistake.why: *Closing* would mean the eyes were in the process of closing; for a finished state, use the past participle.

entries.term: absolute construction: Weather permitting, …
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: A noun + participle with its own subject, and no *with*, gives a condition or background: *Weather permitting, we'll eat outside* means *if the weather allows it*.
entries.usage: Mostly formal or literary, but a few fixed forms are common in everyday speech: *weather permitting, time permitting, all things considered*. In other cases, everyday English adds *with* or uses a full clause (*With the work done, …*).
entries.pattern: noun + participle (+ …), main clause
examples: **Weather permitting**, the fireworks will start at nine over the lake.
**All things considered**, the move went much better than we'd feared.
**Her voice shaking**, she read her father's letter aloud at the funeral.

drill.sentence: {{Time permitting}}, we'll stop at the outlet mall on the way back.
drill.hint: Rewrite with a fixed absolute phrase: If there's enough time, we'll stop at the outlet mall on the way back.

mistake.wrong: Weather permits, we'll go hiking on Sunday.
mistake.right: Weather permitting, we'll go hiking on Sunday.
mistake.why: Without a conjunction, the verb must be a participle (*weather permitting*); otherwise use a full clause (*if the weather permits*).

entries.term: what with …: What with work and the kids, …
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: Introduces several reasons together, usually for stress, tiredness or a problem: *What with work and the kids, I never have time to read.*
entries.usage: Informal and conversational; it often sounds like a sigh or a mild complaint. It is followed by nouns or *-ing* forms, often two joined by *and*, and sometimes ends with *and all*. The main clause states the result, so it needs no *so*.
entries.pattern: What with + noun / -ing (and + noun / -ing), main clause
examples: **What with** the new baby **and** the move, we haven't slept properly in months.
**What with** the rain **and** the traffic, it took us three hours to get home.
I'm not surprised she's tired, **what with** working two jobs and taking night classes.

drill.sentence: {{What with}} the holidays and my sister's wedding, December was exhausting.
drill.hint: Rewrite as a casual complaint: Because of the holidays and my sister's wedding, December was exhausting.

mistake.wrong: What with the rain and the traffic, so we arrived late.
mistake.right: What with the rain and the traffic, we arrived late.
mistake.why: *What with* already gives the reason, so the main clause does not need *so*.

entries.term: so as a clause substitute: I think so / I suppose so
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: After *think, suppose, guess, hope, expect, believe* and *be afraid*, *so* replaces a whole positive clause: *Is she coming? – I think so* means *I think she is coming*.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation, where it saves repeating a whole clause. The verb sets the tone: *I think so* and *I believe so* are neutral, *I guess so* and *I suppose so* often sound reluctant, and *I'm afraid so* gives bad news politely. After *know* and *be sure*, there is no *so*: say *I know* or *I'm not sure*.
entries.pattern: think / believe / suppose / guess / hope / expect / be afraid + so
examples: "Is the pharmacy open on Sundays?" "**I think so**, but call first to be sure."
"Do we really have to invite your cousin?" "**I suppose so**. It would be rude not to."
"Is our flight canceled?" "**I'm afraid so**. They're rebooking everyone for tomorrow."

drill.sentence: "Does the hotel have free parking?" "{{I believe so}}, but I'll double-check when I call them."
drill.hint: Answer briefly, replacing the clause: I believe it does.

mistake.wrong: "Is Mark coming to the party?" "I think yes."
mistake.right: "Is Mark coming to the party?" "I think so."
mistake.why: English uses *so*, not *yes*, to stand for the clause: *I think so*, *I hope so*.

entries.term: So I hear / So it seems
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: Fronted *so* confirms that what someone just said is already known or seems true: *Tom's moving to Denver. – So I hear* means *Yes, I've heard that*.
entries.usage: Conversational, and often dry or slightly ironic. Common forms are *So I hear*, *So I heard*, *So it seems*, *So I see* and *So I've been told*. The subject comes before the verb, with no inversion, which is the difference from *So do I* (*me too*).
entries.pattern: So + subject + hear / see / seem / have been told
examples: "Jake and Emma are finally getting married." "**So I hear**. It's about time!"
"The heat wave is supposed to last all week." "**So it seems**; the forecast keeps getting worse."
"I've been really busy lately." "**So I see**. Your desk is buried in paperwork."

drill.sentence: "Our landlord is selling the building." "{{So I hear}}. Any idea who's buying it?"
drill.hint: Confirm with a short reply (present tense): Yes, I've heard that.

mistake.wrong: "Mark got the job." "So do I hear."
mistake.right: "Mark got the job." "So I hear."
mistake.why: This *so* confirms a fact, so there is no inversion; *So do I* means *me too*.

entries.term: do so: She asked me to leave, and I did so
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *Do so* replaces a verb phrase that was just mentioned, so it does not have to be repeated: *She asked me to leave, and I did so* means *and I left*.
entries.usage: Formal and written: legal texts, official instructions, news and academic writing. In conversation, people use a bare auxiliary (*and I did*) or *do it* / *do that*. It replaces actions, not states: *She owns a car, and I do too*, not *I do so too*.
entries.pattern: subject + (modal) + do so
examples: Passengers who wish to change seats may **do so** after takeoff.
If you haven't renewed your car registration yet, please **do so** before March 31.
The company promised to refund every customer and **did so** within a week.

drill.sentence: Guests who want to check out late may {{do so}} for a fee of $30.
drill.hint: Avoid repeating the verb phrase (formal): Guests who want to check out late may check out late for a fee of $30.

mistake.wrong: "Can you grab me a coffee?" "Sure, I'll do so."
mistake.right: "Can you grab me a coffee?" "Sure, I can do that."
mistake.why: *Do so* is formal and sounds stiff in conversation; use *do that*, *do it* or a bare auxiliary.

entries.term: in doing so
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: Means *by doing this*: it links an action to its result or side effect: *She refused the offer and, in doing so, lost her chance.*
entries.usage: Formal; common in academic writing, news and speeches. The subject of the result must be the person or group who did the action. *In so doing* means the same and sounds even more formal; in conversation people say *and that way* or *by doing that*.
entries.pattern: subject + verb … and, in doing so, (same subject) + result
examples: The city closed Main Street to cars and, **in doing so**, created a popular new public space.
We simplified the data pipeline and, **in doing so**, cut our cloud costs in half.
She told the police what she had seen, and **in doing so** she put herself at risk.

drill.sentence: He sold his car and, {{in doing so}}, saved more than $400 a month.
drill.hint: Link the action to its effect with in + -ing (not *in so doing*): He sold his car. By doing that, he saved more than $400 a month.

mistake.wrong: The team changed suppliers and, in doing so, costs fell by 20 percent.
mistake.right: The team changed suppliers and, in doing so, cut costs by 20 percent.
mistake.why: The result must have the same subject as the action: the team changed suppliers, so the team cut costs.

entries.term: So do I / Neither do I (vs. me too / me neither)
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: Agrees with what someone has said, positive (*So do I*) or negative (*Neither do I*); the auxiliary mirrors the verb in the first statement: *I've been there. – So have I.*
entries.usage: Neutral; in conversation, *Me too* and *Me neither* are more casual and more common. The auxiliary must match the tense and verb of the first statement: *So am I*, *So did I*, *Neither can I*, *Neither have I*. *Nor do I* means the same as *Neither do I* and sounds slightly more formal.
entries.pattern: So / Neither / Nor + auxiliary + subject
examples: "I'm starving." "**So am I**. Let's get something to eat."
"I didn't understand a word of that lecture." "**Neither did I**."
My wife has never been to Europe, and **neither have I**.

drill.sentence: "I can't stand reality TV." "{{Neither can I}}. Let's watch a movie instead."
drill.hint: Agree with inversion (not *nor*): I can't stand it either.

mistake.wrong: "I loved the movie." "So do I."
mistake.right: "I loved the movie." "So did I."
mistake.why: The auxiliary must match the tense of the first statement: *loved* becomes *did*.

entries.term: me either (US informal)
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: An informal American way to agree with a negative statement, with the same meaning as *me neither*: *I don't like olives. – Me either.*
entries.usage: Very common in relaxed American speech and texting; British speakers rarely use it. Traditional grammar calls it illogical, because *either* normally needs a negative verb (*I don't either*), but it is normal in informal US English. In emails and other writing, *neither do I* or *I don't either* is safer.
entries.pattern: negative statement → Me either. (= Me neither / I don't either)
examples: "I don't really feel like cooking tonight." "**Me either**. Let's order Thai."
"I've never seen this much snow in April." "**Me either**!"
"I can't find a parking spot anywhere." "**Me either**; I've been circling for twenty minutes."

drill.sentence: "I'm not a big fan of musicals." "{{Me either}}. Can we pick something else?"
drill.hint: Agree casually, American style (not *me neither*): I'm not a fan either.

mistake.wrong: "I love this song." "Me either!"
mistake.right: "I love this song." "Me too!"
mistake.why: *Me either* only agrees with a negative statement; after a positive one, say *me too*.

entries.term: that of / those of: higher than that of Japan
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *That of* (singular) and *those of* (plural) replace a noun that would otherwise be repeated in a comparison: *Its population is larger than that of Japan* means *than the population of Japan*.
entries.usage: Formal; common in academic, legal and news writing. Careful writers use it to compare like with like (a climate with a climate, not with a city), and choose *that* or *those* to match the noun. In speech, people usually use a possessive instead (*than Japan's*).
entries.pattern: noun … than / as / to + that of / those of + noun
examples: The cost of living in Boston is much higher than **that of** most American cities.
Her symptoms were very similar to **those of** a mild flu.
The new model's accuracy is close to **that of** trained human experts.

drill.sentence: Teachers' salaries in this state are lower than {{those of}} teachers in neighboring states.
drill.hint: Avoid repeating the plural noun (formal): Teachers' salaries in this state are lower than the salaries of teachers in neighboring states.

mistake.wrong: The climate of Seattle is milder than Chicago.
mistake.right: The climate of Seattle is milder than that of Chicago.
mistake.why: In careful writing, compare like with like: a climate with a climate, so *that of* stands for *the climate of* (or say *Chicago's*).

entries.term: the former / the latter
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *The former* refers to the first of two things just mentioned, and *the latter* to the second: *We looked at Denver and Austin and chose the latter* (Austin).
entries.usage: Formal and mainly written; in speech people usually repeat the noun or say *the first one* and *the second one*. Traditionally it is used for exactly two items; with three or more, *the first* or *the last* is clearer. Use it only when the two items are short and close, so the reader doesn't have to look back.
entries.pattern: A and B …; the former (= A) / the latter (= B) …
examples: We had to choose between a bigger apartment and a shorter commute, and we went with **the latter**.
Wolves and coyotes both live in the park, but **the former** are rarely seen by visitors.
You can pay in full now or in monthly installments; most customers choose **the former**.

drill.sentence: We could take the train or rent a car. {{The former}} is cheaper, but the latter is faster.
drill.hint: Refer back without repeating the noun: We could take the train or rent a car. The train is cheaper, but the car is faster.

mistake.wrong: We looked at two cars and bought the later.
mistake.right: We looked at two cars and bought the latter.
mistake.why: *Latter* (double *t*, /ˈlætɚ/) means the second of two; *later* means at a later time.

entries.term: whatever clause: Whatever you decide, …
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: A *whatever*-clause says that the main clause is true in every case: *Whatever you decide, I'll support you* means *no matter what you decide*.
entries.usage: Common in speech and writing; *no matter what* means the same and is a bit more emphatic. The clause usually comes first, followed by a comma, and uses the present tense for future meaning (*Whatever happens, …*). *Whatever you do* + an imperative is a common spoken warning (*Whatever you do, don't …*).
entries.pattern: Whatever + subject + verb, main clause
examples: **Whatever you order**, save room for the peach pie.
**Whatever happens** in the final, this has been an amazing season.
**Whatever you do**, don't mention the wedding in front of her mother.

drill.sentence: {{Whatever she wears}}, she always looks great.
drill.hint: Rewrite with whatever: It doesn't matter what she wears; she always looks great.

mistake.wrong: What you decide, I'll support you.
mistake.right: Whatever you decide, I'll support you.
mistake.why: *What* alone does not mean *no matter what*; use *whatever* or *no matter what*.

entries.term: verbless whatever: Whatever the reason, …
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *Whatever* + a noun phrase, with no verb, means *whatever the X is or was*: *Whatever the reason, he never called back.*
entries.usage: Common in writing and also in speech, mostly in set phrases: *whatever the reason, whatever the cost, whatever the outcome, whatever the weather*. It sounds compact and slightly formal. A verb can follow the noun (*whatever the reason is*, *whatever the reason may be*), but it does not go between *whatever* and the noun.
entries.pattern: Whatever + the + noun, main clause / main clause, whatever + the + noun
examples: **Whatever the reason**, she hasn't spoken to her brother in years.
We're going to the beach on Saturday, **whatever the weather**.
**Whatever the outcome** of the trial, the family says it just wants answers.

drill.sentence: {{Whatever the cost}}, we need to fix the roof before winter.
drill.hint: Shorten with whatever + noun: No matter what it costs, we need to fix the roof before winter.

mistake.wrong: Whatever is the reason, it's not your fault.
mistake.right: Whatever the reason, it's not your fault.
mistake.why: Either drop the verb (*whatever the reason*) or put it after the noun (*whatever the reason is*).

entries.term: however + adjective: However hard I try, …
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *However* + adjective or adverb means *no matter how*: *However hard I try, I can't remember her name.*
entries.usage: Neutral to formal; *no matter how* is more common in speech. The adjective or adverb must come directly after *however*, before the subject, and formal style sometimes adds *may* (*however tempting it may be*). Do not confuse it with *however* meaning *but*, which is followed by a comma.
entries.pattern: However + adjective / adverb / much / many + subject + verb, main clause
examples: **However hard I try**, I can't get my sourdough to rise properly.
We'll find a way to pay for college, **however long** it takes.
**However tempting** it may be, don't reply to that email tonight.

drill.sentence: {{However busy he is}}, he always calls his mother on Sundays.
drill.hint: Rewrite with however, at the start: He always calls his mother on Sundays, no matter how busy he is.

mistake.wrong: However I try hard, I can't understand him.
mistake.right: However hard I try, I can't understand him.
mistake.why: The adjective or adverb comes right after *however*, before the subject.

entries.term: whoever as a noun clause: Whoever did this …
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *Whoever* + clause means *the person who* or *any person who*, and the whole clause works as a subject or an object: *Whoever did this owes me an apology.*
entries.usage: Common in speech and writing, often when the person is unknown (*Whoever took my lunch …*) or when anyone at all is meant (*Invite whoever you want*). In practice *whoever* is used in almost every position; *whomever* is formal and rare, and is often used wrongly where the word is the subject of its own clause.
entries.pattern: Whoever + verb … + main verb / verb or preposition + whoever + clause
examples: **Whoever** ate my leftovers from the fridge owes me lunch.
You can bring **whoever you want** to the barbecue.
**Whoever** gets home first starts dinner; that's the rule in our house.

drill.sentence: Give the extra tickets to {{whoever}} wants them.
drill.hint: Choose whoever or whomever: Give the extra tickets to ___ wants them.

mistake.wrong: Who wants to join us is welcome.
mistake.right: Whoever wants to join us is welcome.
mistake.why: In modern English, *who* alone cannot start a subject clause meaning *anyone who*; use *whoever* or *anyone who*.

entries.term: whereby
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: A formal relative word meaning *by which* or *under which*; it describes how a system, method or arrangement works: *a plan whereby employees can buy shares*.
entries.usage: Typical of formal writing: contracts, policy documents, reports and academic texts. It nearly always follows a noun like *system, process, arrangement, scheme, mechanism* or *agreement*. In everyday English, people use *where*, *in which* or a different sentence (*a plan that lets employees buy shares*).
entries.pattern: system / process / arrangement / agreement + whereby + clause
examples: The two neighbors have an informal arrangement **whereby** one mows both lawns and the other shovels the snow.
The city introduced a system **whereby** residents can report potholes through an app.
Photosynthesis is the process **whereby** plants turn sunlight into chemical energy.

drill.sentence: The bank offers a plan {{whereby}} customers can skip one payment a year.
drill.hint: Make it formal (one word): The bank offers a plan in which customers can skip one payment a year.

mistake.wrong: This is the restaurant whereby we had our first date.
mistake.right: This is the restaurant where we had our first date.
mistake.why: *Whereby* means *by means of which* and describes systems or arrangements, not places.

entries.term: preposition + which: the extent to which
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: In formal English, the preposition of a relative clause moves in front of *which*: *the extent to which*, *the rate at which*, *the house in which they lived*.
entries.usage: Typical of academic, legal and news writing. Some phrases are almost always used this way (*the extent to which*, *the degree to which*, *the rate at which*, *the way in which*). In conversation, the preposition usually goes to the end and *which* is dropped (*the house they lived in*).
entries.pattern: noun + preposition + which + subject + verb
examples: It's hard to know **the extent to which** the drought will push up food prices.
Doctors are worried about **the rate at which** the infection is spreading.
The farmhouse **in which** my grandparents lived is now a small museum.

drill.sentence: Nobody knows yet {{the extent to which}} the new law will change daily life.
drill.hint: Make it formal, with extent: Nobody knows yet how much the new law will change daily life.

mistake.wrong: This is the town in which I grew up in.
mistake.right: This is the town in which I grew up.
mistake.why: The preposition appears only once: either before *which* or at the end (*the town I grew up in*).

entries.term: the way (that), not 'the way how'
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: To talk about the manner of doing something, use *the way (that)* or *how*, but not both together: *I love the way you cook* or *I love how you cook*.
entries.usage: Very common in speech and writing. *The way* can be followed by *that*, by *in which* (formal) or directly by the clause; *the way how* is an old form that sounds wrong today. *How* alone is often shorter and just as natural.
entries.pattern: the way (that / in which) + clause / how + clause
examples: I love **the way** she laughs at her own jokes.
That's not **the way** we do things around here.
**The way** the city handled the snowstorm was a complete disaster.

drill.sentence: I don't like {{the way}} he talks to the waitstaff.
drill.hint: Correct the sentence, keeping *the way*: I don't like the way how he talks to the waitstaff.

mistake.wrong: This is the way how we fixed it.
mistake.right: This is the way we fixed it.
mistake.why: Use *the way* or *how*, never both together.

entries.term: at which point
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: Means *and at that moment*: it links an event to what happened next, often a turning point: *The power went out, at which point everyone started screaming.*
entries.usage: Common in stories, both spoken and written, and in step-by-step explanations (*… until the water boils, at which point you add the pasta*). It follows a comma and refers to the moment described in the whole previous clause. It is more vivid than *then* and often marks a surprise.
entries.pattern: clause, at which point + clause
examples: We argued for twenty minutes, **at which point** the waiter politely asked us to leave.
Stir the sauce until it thickens, **at which point** you can add the cheese.
The Hawks led until the last two minutes, **at which point** everything fell apart.

drill.sentence: The baby finally fell asleep, {{at which point}} the doorbell rang.
drill.hint: Join the two events: The baby finally fell asleep. At that exact moment, the doorbell rang.

mistake.wrong: The music stopped, in which point everyone went home.
mistake.right: The music stopped, at which point everyone went home.
mistake.why: A moment in time takes *at* (*at that point*), so the relative form is *at which point*.

entries.term: quantifier + of whom / of which: some of whom
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: A quantifier + *of whom* (people) or *of which* (things) starts a relative clause about part of a group: *forty guests, most of whom were family*.
entries.usage: Typical of writing and formal speech; in conversation people usually start a new clause (*and most of them were family*). Common words before it are *some, many, most, all, none, both, neither, half* and numbers. It follows a comma, and *who* or *them* cannot replace *whom* here.
entries.pattern: noun, + quantifier / number + of whom / of which + verb
examples: We invited forty people, **most of whom** were family.
She has three brothers, **all of whom** live within ten miles of their parents.
The shop sells hundreds of cheeses, **some of which** I had never even heard of.

drill.sentence: The museum has twelve rooms, {{two of which}} are closed for repairs.
drill.hint: Join with a relative clause: The museum has twelve rooms, and two of them are closed for repairs.

mistake.wrong: I have two sisters, both of them live in Texas.
mistake.right: I have two sisters, both of whom live in Texas.
mistake.why: Without *and*, the second clause must be a relative clause: *both of whom*, not *both of them*.

entries.term: stranded preposition vs. fronting: who I spoke to / to whom I spoke
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: In most English, the preposition of a relative clause or question goes at the end (*the person I spoke to*); moving it to the front with *whom* or *which* (*the person to whom I spoke*) is formal.
entries.usage: Ending a sentence with a preposition is normal and correct in all registers; the rule against it is a myth. Fronting is used in formal writing, but it doesn't work with phrasal verbs (*the problem we ran into*, not *into which we ran*). After a fronted preposition, only *whom* is possible for people (*to whom*, not *to who*).
entries.pattern: (who / that / Ø) … + preposition at the end (normal) / preposition + whom / which … (formal)
examples: Is that the guy **you were talking to** at the party?
The committee will decide **to whom** the scholarship should be awarded.
What are you so worried **about**? The test isn't until next week.

drill.sentence: She's the friend {{I traveled to Peru with}} after college.
drill.hint: Make it less formal by moving the preposition to the end: She's the friend with whom I traveled to Peru after college.

mistake.wrong: The neighbor to who I lent my ladder never returned it.
mistake.right: The neighbor to whom I lent my ladder never returned it.
mistake.why: Directly after a preposition, only *whom* is possible; if you prefer *who*, move the preposition to the end.

entries.term: whether vs. if in noun clauses
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: Both introduce yes/no noun clauses (*I don't know whether / if she's coming*), but careful English uses only *whether* after a preposition, before a *to*-infinitive and as the subject.
entries.usage: In everyday speech, *if* is more common after *ask, know, wonder* and *see*. Use *whether* before a *to*-infinitive (*whether to stay*), as the subject (*Whether he knew is unclear*) and right before *or not*. After prepositions, *if* is heard in casual speech (*It depends on if …*), but *whether* is the standard choice.
entries.pattern: after a preposition, before to + verb, as subject, before or not → whether; after ask / know / wonder → whether or if
examples: The picnic depends on **whether** the weather holds.
We're still trying to decide **whether to** rent or buy.
**Whether** he knew about the problem is still unclear.

drill.sentence: {{Whether}} we go camping this weekend depends on the forecast.
drill.hint: Choose whether or if (the clause is the subject): ___ we go camping this weekend depends on the forecast.

mistake.wrong: I don't know if to take the job in Phoenix.
mistake.right: I don't know whether to take the job in Phoenix.
mistake.why: Before a *to*-infinitive, only *whether* is possible.
